  lifetime in advance and allocate from a region, which is why the oldest idea in the field — the stack — keeps
  returning under new names whenever performance genuinely matters.

  The reason any of this works remains the empirical fact that the worst case never arrives. A general-purpose
  allocator is a bet that the program requesting memory behaves like most programs: that it uses few distinct
  sizes, that objects allocated together die together, that most objects are small and short-lived, and that
  allocation and deallocation are roughly balanced within a phase. Allocators that fit those regularities
  tightly achieve a few percent overhead against a theoretical bound that permits catastrophic waste. When a
  program violates the assumptions — allocating a huge span of sizes, holding one small object alive on every
  page, or moving memory systematically between threads — the results degrade in ways that look like bugs but
  are really the bet being lost. Which is why the practical advice at the end of this history is the same as it
  was at the beginning: if you know something specific about your program's lifetimes, encode it directly in an
  arena or a pool, and leave the general-purpose allocator for the cases where you genuinely do not.

✻ Sautéed for 3m 55s
